newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Ugly Singaporean strikes again.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ugly Singaporean strikes again.

text.p: A rusty washing machine, a badly stained armchair and old, dirty and broken toys were donated by Singaporeans to charity last Christmas.
This came barely a year after a public uproar against some well-off Singaporeans jostling for free books meant for poor children.
The incidents highlighted the ugly, ungracious side of Singapore which the city-state is trying very hard to shed as it joins the ranks of developed nations.
"There were incomplete game sets, toy aeroplanes without wings, and dolls without arms," Desmond Koh, a Christmas charity organiser, told the Straits Times newspaper.
"These are things we would never give our own children. Some were so dirty and dusty that it was obvious the people were just trying to get rid of them."
At the giveaway of school textbooks in 1995, parents among the 800-strong crowd pushed, yelled and bickered as they scrambled to snap up some 80,000 used books.
The stampede for freebies helped prompt Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong to announce that his government would focus on upgrading social graciousness over the next few years.
TRY A LITTLE KINDNESS
In his New Year message in 1996 Goh said some Singaporeans "still behave as if they were in the Stone Age" and called for a more gracious approach to life.

Returning to the same theme last August on the eve of the nation's 31st birthday, Goh said, "Singaporeans cannot just be materialistic, self-centred and impatient to get rich quick. My vision is a Singapore where every citizen strives to make Singapore a better home."
In response to Goh's appeal, the city-state launched a "Small Kindness Movement" to make random acts of kindness second nature to its busy citizens.
It was renamed "Singapore Kindness Movement" on February 3 and given a logo, so Singaporeans could better identify with the campaign.
"We hope to spread the awareness that individuals have the ability to grace people around us with simple acts of kindness," its chairman Noel Hon said.
"A gracious society is only possible if we are willing to think beyond ourselves and to show consideration for others."
MONEY OVER GRACE
But some Singaporeans feel that their preoccupation with acquiring material wealth makes it difficult for them to put others first.

"There is so much emphasis on getting the five Cs (condominium, car, career, credit card, cash) that I don't have time to think of other people," said Denny Tan, a commodity trader. "I don't want to be left behind."

At its most extreme, a "me-first" attitude goes some way in explaining anti-social behaviour in the city-state, which recently included throwing bulky objects from high-rise flats and parking vehicles in places reserved for the handicapped.
In an effort to get people to mend their ways, the local media ran a high-profile campaign to expose the able-bodied who parked in such lots.
The series of articles and photographs, complete with the vehicles' registration numbers, angered the public, prompting calls for tougher action against those who parked illegally.
"Many of these selfish drivers managed to have their fines waived by the authorities after they had given their explanation," Jack Goh wrote in the Straits Times.
"It would seem that the authorities have failed to tackle the problem effectively."
AN EXCEPTION RATHER THAN THE RULE?
But others argued that there will always be a few bad apples. "You always have a small proportion of Singaporeans who do not think properly," Hon told Reuters.
"The majority of Singaporeans would like to see a more caring society. That there is outcry and anger that such things occur shows that society does not accept such behaviour."
Hon noted that Singaporeans are better behaved these days.
"A year ago (1995) there was a rush for books but this year the same thing did not occur," he said.
But others said the main factor preventing a stampede was better organisation, which they said was also a reason for Singapore's squeaky clean public areas.
"Our streets are clean not because Singaporeans do not litter but because we have an army of cleaners," said Albert Lim, a 35-year old executive.
